By Rory Fenton

Published on October 8, 2026 5:40 PM GMT

Cross-posted from my Substack.

Epistemic status: I’ve puzzled over this for a long time but I’m not sure I came to the right answers. I'm sharing this partly because it might help others work on resource allocation, but mostly because some smarter reader might tell me how to do it better.

TL;DR:

  • I helped set up a large foundation and we wanted a consistent way to allocate grants
  • We planned to allocate substantially more than our field was able to absorb right now, giving us the opportunity to actively shape our field
  • We outlined key principles and considerations
  • We quickly learned we could not just copy the for-profit world: so what could we do?
  • We could try and optimize perfectly, mathematically, but it gets absurd and impractical
  • Instead, we tried out a bunch of different approaches to finding a consistent grant allocation formula, settling on the one that most “felt” right given our starting principles and constraints
  • I quite liked this process of setting principles and constraints, and then vibing your way to an allocation formula that feels right vs being super mathematical
  • I wanted to share this process as a real example of trying to work out how to allocate funding. It might be useful to people in the same position, or people might have ideas for how we could have done better 

x = height of the opposing player

When I was about 10, I started to learn algebra in school. Clearly a future EA, I had a brainwave on my way home one day: I can use this new math to become really good at Goldeneye, an N64 shooting game. I got increasingly excited as I walked downhill home, imagining myself briefly pausing the game, whipping out my notebook, firing off some calculations, and then, BAM, quick console controller movements would finish off my nemeses with the precision only numbers could provide. 

So I got home, opened my notebook, and wrote “x = height of opposing player”.

I paused.

I paused longer.

"Eugh"

I closed my notebook and gave up. 

I hadn’t been entirely wrong to try. In principle, there are optimal moves at any given moment that can maximize your chances of winning any game, and those can indeed be identified mathematically. But my 10-year-old brain realized the absurdity of computing all of my actions on paper, while constantly updating the calculations as the game progressed. 

But this post isn’t about Nintendo, it’s about doing as much good as possible with limited resources. 

Searching for the perfect grant-allocation formula

A few years ago I helped set up a private foundation aiming to spend a few hundred million dollars over the coming years on global development. There is a staggering responsibility to spend that money effectively. As we planned our first year (a few $10ms in grants), I thought a lot about how to allocate funding to very different organizations under quite a bit of uncertainty on grantee potential. I didn’t solve it, but I ended up getting to a place that was good enough to begin. Maybe it’s useful, especially if you are working out how to spend sums that your field is not currently ready to absorb.

Our core metrics

  1. Cost-effectiveness based on historic performance and discounted for evidence quality (i.e. we preferred large scale RCTs to pre/post studies of small pilots)
  2. Chance of success defined by the % chance they would exceed our minimum cost-effectiveness bar. Obviously the higher our cost-effectiveness estimate, the higher their chance of success, but this allowed us to factor in other things like “expanding to a new country”, “impressive new CEO” and “need to hire a new, unproven team” that would not be included in the cost-effectiveness estimate, which was based on historic impact assessments

These metrics allowed for a neat division of labor. The cost-effectiveness estimate would be fully owned by the research team, while the % success estimates would be owned by the programs team.

Setting metrics was the easy part, the hard part was working out how to turn those numbers into a neat “Give Org A $3m this year” output. 

We couldn’t just copy from other grantmakers or the for-profit world

Hold on, you might say, can’t you just copy the funding allocation model of [one of the famous big EA grant makers]. Surprisingly, at least a few years ago, no org I spoke to had a formula that says how much to allocate to a given opportunity. More common is to see if the opportunity passes your funding bar and fund it if it does, but there is no formula that says “we ideally would give this org $xM”, with the grant sizing generally left to the grantee to request. 

Our case was also unique in that we had more money to spend than grantees in our field could currently absorb, and so we were in the position of building our field rather than just allocating to the opportunities that existed in front of us. We had the ability to support the most promising grantees to grow to absorb more, meaning we didn't need to simply "rank everyone by cost-effectiveness and give them as much money as they can take, starting at the top". We wanted to answer "how much would this grantee ideally take?".

So I turned to the VC/hedge fund world for inspiration. But I gradually realized that there are some fundamental differences between for-profit investment and grant-making that prevented us from simply copy-pasting from a hedge fund.

Non-profit funders are not penalized for missing amazing start-ups: A for-profit investor will be penalized for missing a great start-up by paying much more for the same share later on e.g. an investor buying shares in Uber in 2020 will really wish she had invested in Uber in 2010. 

Grant-making doesn’t work this way: if I'm faced with a high-risk/reward non-profit, I can give them a small grant, learn if they do a good job with it, and then donate more, later, once my confidence is higher. All else equal, I don't take a hit on impact from waiting, but I do reduce my risk. 

Non-profits don’t have to optimize for keeping their pot of money: A failed for-profit investment is more damaging than the immediate loss: if I lose a $100k investment, not only have I lost $100k, I’ve lost the compounding profits that that $100k could have made if I hadn’t lost it and been able to invest in future opportunities. What's more, a total failure will lead to going bankrupt and entirely prevent future investments. This dynamic will lead to rational for-profit investors being somewhat risk averse: you don’t want to risk losing your money and not longer being able to play the game, which typically results in investments being spread around opportunities of varying risk/reward rather than betting on just one amazing opportunity. 

But a successful $100k grant costs a grant-maker just as much as an unsuccessful $100k: it costs $100k. All things equal, this makes it easier to take risks with grants that you might not want to take with for-profit investments

Note that the 2 dynamics above are somewhat at odds with each other. The former points to being less aggressive with high risk/reward opportunities since you can just wait until you have better information. The latter points to being more risk tolerant since you aren’t trying to maintain your pot of funding. The later sections will talk more about how we tried to balance these dynamics.[1] 

Turning our principles into a utility function + optimizing

We wanted to generally maximize impact, but with some risk aversion and spreading of bets, both because we could adjust our funding over time as our confidence levels changed but also because this was our first year of grant-making, and if we totally failed to generate impact, our donors might just drop us. 

If we wanted to present that mathematically, we could model the implied utility function (roughly, "How excited are we by a particular grant") as a linear combination of:

  • Maximize utility: Utility is linear with funding*cost-effectiveness
  • Better to spread bets: Utility grows at, say, the logarithm of funding invested into each opportunity. So we want to put more into good opportunities but the more we’ve already put in, the less attractive those opportunities get
  • Delay funding for risky bets: An aggressive function like 1-f - f^2, where f is the probability of failure, would penalize high risk. This looks pretty linear at smaller risk levels, but rapidly drops to zero/negative utility if the risk goes above a threshold, incenvitizing us to wait for the risk to drop before spending more

We could then bring this all together into a single utility function, like AX + B ln(X + C) -D f- Df^2, where X is the funding allocated, f is risk, and A is cost-effectiveness, and B, C, and D would be constants that we could all align on through internal conversations and talking to our funders, based on how we valued risk. 

Except… this all felt a lot like 10-year-old me writing “x= height of opposing player”. What numbers could we possibly substitute for B, C, and D that had any meaningful bearing on reality? That wouldn’t change as soon as we made our first grants and started learning about just how wide our error bars had always been?

So, and I will not pretend to have had a grand strategy behind this, we simply tried out a bunch of different methods for allocating funding using our key metrics, to see if we could tell if any “felt” more right than the others.  

“Vibing” our way to a utility function 

Here are toy examples based on our real grantees. If you want to play along, I suggest taking a look at these first and thinking through how you might allocate $30m:

Below, I’ll walk through the different allocation strategies we considered for our first $30m in grants, along with the gut reactions from colleagues and internal discussions.

The "Obvious" Option: Allocate by Expected Cost-Effectiveness

Straightforward enough. Multiply the cost-effectiveness by probability of success, get an expected return, allocate proportionally. Here’s how that would look for some example grantees:

 

“Impact” here is just put into generic units, you could imagine something like “lives saved”, “DALYs averted”, etc

This approach felt wrong. It pushed us to spend large sums on orgs that felt quite high risk, when we knew that with a smaller grant we could learn more about their chances of success and choose to go bigger next year– it actually wasn’t optimal to go big immediately if we could gain more confidence in our higher risk investments first. 

The "Risk-Buckets" Approach

The Risk Buckets idea was a reaction to the above. With Risk Buckets allocate funds into different buckets based on risk levels, then optimize within each bucket for cost-effectiveness. This would enable us to avoid going big on higher-risk grants by learning first with a smaller grant. 

We tried something like this:

… which would lead to funding allocation like this:

We didn’t love it. We were left with the opposite problem from our first approach: we were allocating a lot of money to things we didn't think would deliver lots of impact, just because they were safe. 

The Kelly Criterion

Originating in finance, Kelly tells you the optimal fraction of your funds to bet on opportunities based on risk and reward. I first encountered it through Michael Lewis's book on Sam Bankman-Fried, who notably rejected Kelly as too conservative.

Kelly’s formula: optimal allocation (%) = success rate (%) - [(failure rate %) / (return per dollar)]. On paper, it looked ideal, directly optimizing risk vs. reward trade-offs. Also it came from finance, and finance is cool.

Here’s what a Kelly-optimized grant portfolio would look like for us:

But Kelly has a crucial assumption: you’re growing an investment portfolio where losses directly reduce your available capital, your ability to keep playing the game. In grant-making, if a grant fails or succeeds, you lose the grant money either way, as discussed earlier. This causes Kelly to be overly cautious for grantmaking, pushing too much toward low-risk, low-return bets. For example, something like Org F (high success chance (75%) but modest cost-effectiveness) still received outsized allocations ($3m). Kelly optimized for "not going broke," a constraint that people giving money away for free don’t have. 

Sharpe ratio

The Sharpe ratio is another concept from the finance world. It allows for a risk-adjusted estimate of the value of an opportunity and is calculated by taking the expected return, minus a risk-free return (like government bonds), all divided by the standard deviation of the portfolio's excess returns (vs risk-free). The idea of meaningfully estimating the standard deviation of excess returns of a bunch of nonprofits with varying data quality seemed pretty unrealistic. We did not pursue the Sharpe ratio further.

Edge

Finally, through Nate Silver's book "On the Edge," I encountered "edge," a poker player's heuristic defined as the return to success divided by odds of failure. This is very similar to Kelly, but because it uses odds rather than percentages, it subtly nudges towards higher-risk, higher-reward opportunities.

Here’s how paying grants in proportion to edge looked for us:

The initial consensus of colleagues? This feels right! By funding in proportion to edge, we had a straightforward way of being cautious with high-risk investments but ambitious with promising investments. Importantly, none of the recommended grants felt very off, though some recommendations came off as useful challenges (“Huh, the edge is high and I guess we could go bigger with those guys”).

Here’s how all of the strategies look together: 

What We Actually Did

We really liked the use of edge to generate an initial grant recommendation, subject to occasional adjustment based on “gut”, but adjustment wasn’t common. 

Surprisingly, the biggest benefit was psychological. The concept of edge generated a useful tool for our program officers as they engaged (potential) grantees, focusing conversations around estimating and increasing our "edge". Seeking opportunities to boost and balance cost-effectiveness and probability of success. 

I left the org (Prevail Fund) a few years ago and from catching up with colleagues, the concept of edge ended up most useful for our early years of grants and less relevant to our longer term state, which was more of a "repeatable game" with clearer data on each grantee. 

If we settled on edge, doesn’t that mean there was a calculable utility function in the background the whole time?

You could reasonably point out that the approach we took of trying out different methods until we found one that “felt” right was really just a trial-and-error way of identifying our underlying utility function, which is fundamentally still a mathematical object. And you’d be right! In fact, you can write out the “edge” formula and integrate it to identify the implied utility function that it maximes. I gave this a go and graphed it, it looks like this:

item.title: CCF: The Spreadsheet in Your Head Is Misallocating Your Giving
item.description:
Published on October 8, 2026 6:18 PM GMT


Opinion piece by Marcus A. Davis, CEO of Rethink Priorities

TL;DR:

  1. The problem: Major donors choose between causes like AI safety, global health, and animal welfare without writing down why. In interviews, many couldn’t say what their gifts achieved or how they weighed one cause against another.
  2. Why it happens: Skipping the spreadsheet feels simpler and more humble, but every gut call is still a model, just one nobody can see or check.
  3. How it goes wrong: The hidden model makes strong claims by accident. An even split says every cause is equally good at the margin. “I’ll adjust a bit for my doubts” could mean very different strategies. Anything you didn’t think about gets counted as zero. A model you only follow when it agrees with you corrects nothing.
  4. Why it gets worse with harder questions: Cross-cause decisions are complex and give no feedback, which is exactly when intuition is least reliable, and mistakes are hardest to notice.
  5. What it costs: Millions can be given with no all-things-considered comparison behind them, so money is likely being misallocated.
  6. What to do: Small donors can rely on a fund or evaluator. Large donors should pay for in-depth analysis, since even a marginally better decision can justify it. Donors in between can use shared analysis rather than building their own. Whatever you rely on, ask it to show its work: which assumptions drive the answer, what’s being counted as zero, and what would change the recommendation.

 

If it’s possible to be famous for your spreadsheets, GiveWell, the charity evaluator, is. To decide whether malaria nets do more good per dollar than deworming pills, they build models with dozens of inputs, such as how many nets are actually used, how common malaria is in each region, and how much a child’s health today affects their earnings decades later.

It’s a heroic effort, built and refined over the last 19 years, that tries to pin down all the uncertainties they have about this complex question.

Now, every so often, someone looks at this complex model and says something like, “Why bother? Malaria kills children. Nets prevent malaria. Worms are bad, but they usually don’t kill you. Nets win. I worked that out in ten seconds from a high-level argument without opening a spreadsheet.”

The problem is that person isn’t truly skipping the spreadsheet. They’ve built one in their head. They just aren’t showing their work, even to themselves.

Congratulations, that was a model

A model is really any story about how an action leads to outcomes. No one opens a spreadsheet to decide when to leave for work. But you have a model: typical traffic, how much lateness you can tolerate, whether it’s raining, and so on. Many people, unfortunately, find out that this is a model when they are an hour late to work because a bridge was closed.

The same issue applies to high-level stories people tell themselves about why to give to one area rather than another or how to split across them. The person assuming “bednets win” has built a model in their head that depends on:

  • Bednets actually being used
  • Malaria being common where the nets go
  • The long-term benefits of deworming being small or unproven, and
  • A child’s life being worth more than a lifetime of somewhat higher income for many children

Each of these is a number. Change a couple, and the answer can flip. GiveWell’s spreadsheet isn’t more complicated structurally than the reasoning underlying the ten-second model. It’s equally complicated, just visible and inspectable.

The lessons here are:

  1. If you disagree with someone’s spreadsheet, you owe them your numbers. “Models are dumb” isn’t a rebuttal when your alternative is a secret model doing computation in your head that can’t be interrogated.
  2. Anything you believe can, in principle, be written down. The real question is whether writing it down loses more than it gains. Usually it gains a lot, and I’m pretty sure cause prioritization is one of those times.

The critics of models have a point, but it doesn’t prove what they think

Some skeptics go further. They don’t just think models are unnecessary; they think models are misleading, and that experienced judgment is the safer guide. They raise some fair points:

  • Point estimates hide uncertainty. Many inputs are best guesses with wide error bars. The evidence might suggest a condition reduces quality of life by about 20%, but with a plausible range anywhere from 5% to 50%. A spreadsheet that just enters “20%” makes the answer look more certain than it is.
  • Averages aren’t everything. Even when the odds are well understood, the average isn’t the whole story. A safe bet that reliably helps 10 people and a long shot with a 1% chance of helping 1,000 have the same average, but many people would reasonably prefer the safe bet.
  • The spreadsheet can’t see what it left out. It can carefully track one effect, like lives saved, while missing another entirely, like effects on the local economy.
  • One wrong input can swing everything. A formula error, or even just a poorly calibrated input, can sometimes flip the result.

All of this is true. Now ask yourself whether the alternative of going with your gut fixes any of these issues. Spoiler: it does not.

Leaving it out is the same as counting it as zero

People worry that explicit models leave out factors or produce results that are too precise. This does happen. But why do you think your unaided mind has captured all the relevant factors in the correct amounts and to the correct level of precision? Our ten-second model critic almost certainly didn’t have region-specific estimates of disease burden, or a clear sense of how much extra future income would be worth as much as saving a life.

But not thinking about something is the same as building a model and counting it as having no effect. And zero is the most confident estimate there is. Leaving something out isn’t humble, it’s maximally sure.

Indeed, an ignored effect gets an estimate of zero, with no error bars. If precision is the concern, the informal approach is the most overconfident.

In more formal models, the alternative to skipping inputs like this is to directly flag where you think the uncertainty is, and test multiple inputs, rather than use a made-up precise number. A spreadsheet can write “unknown, could be big” or “we ran a sensitivity analysis, and this had no effect on our conclusion.” A gut feeling that never noticed the question can’t.

Now let’s try a harder question

You may think I’m being silly. Of course, you think, no one can do GiveWell’s spreadsheets in their head. Don’t be ridiculous. But cause prioritization is different, you might say. You can compare bednets to AI risk interventions without building a formal model. This may sound intuitive, but doing that in your head is harder, not easier.

The more different two interventions are, the more theory- and philosophy-driven your outcomes may be. For example, here’s a line of reasoning that many thoughtful people hold: AI is the most important thing happening in the world right now. If it goes badly, almost nothing else matters. So AI safety is where marginal money does the most good.

Notice what this argument quietly depends on:

  • What an extra dollar does now, in a field that has recently gotten a lot more money and attention. It’s possible that a cause can be the most important in the world, yet the next dollar put into it is not the best use of a dollar.
  • Whether the work helps, some well-intentioned work in a new field can turn out to be neutral or counterproductive. How likely is that, for the work you’d fund?
  • How much of the case rests on a small chance of an enormous outcome, and how comfortable are you with that kind of bet?

People who hold this view have usually thought hard about some of these. The question isn’t whether you’ve considered them. It’s whether you’ve considered all of them, with actual numbers, and how they combine. That last part is where reasoning in your head is least reliable. It’s not at all obvious that the best thing to do is to act on what appears to be the highest-expected-value bet based on a high-level argument when you can’t be confident you are pushing in the right direction. It’s reasonable to give at least some weight to that view, but how much, specifically? And what do you do if you also have views that are more risk-averse, which say you absolutely should not spend money on projects like this?

One option in the case where you hold competing views is “I’ll evenly split across a few causes I care about.” This sounds like the humble option. But an even split is a strong claim: that each cause is roughly equally worth funding at the margin, and that every option on the list does good rather than harm. It’s a model with the weights set to “equal” because nobody wrote down anything else.

“Just adjust a bit” is (hilariously) underspecified

Even simple cases of weighing multiple views are really complicated. Consider a simple case where you have $10 million to spend on philanthropic causes. You’re about 80% confident in a view on which AI safety is far and away the best use of money. You give about 20% to a more cautious view that proven global health programs are best and speculative AI work might even be worse than doing nothing. In this circumstance, some people think, “I’ll just adjust a little,” and assume they’ve reached the right answer. Unfortunately, that move is almost comically underspecified.

“I’ll adjust a bit for the 20%” could mean any of these:

  1. Ignore the 20%: give the $10M to AI safety
  2. Split by confidence: Give $8M to AI safety and $2M to global health
  3. Follow the main view, skip the riskiest bets: $10M to AI safety but only to established, lower-variance options
  4. Find something both theories can live with: Maybe a mix of $5M to animal welfare (which the risk-taking theory likes) and $5M to global health

These aren’t small variations. These are four different philanthropic strategies. “I’ll adjust a bit” doesn’t tell you which one of these you picked. Worse, there are better and worse reasons to pursue each of these moves in different circumstances; they lead to very different practical results, and it’s hard to do (3) or (4) in a consistent way without a formal model.

(1) just ignores your uncertainties. (2) splits resources. (3) and (4) could result in whatever you want based on how you view the “riskiest” choices and some bespoke informal negotiation in your head.

There’s just no reason to think it’s better to do this type of analysis in your head rather than under a formal structure. And this is the easy case, when you are comparing two theories rather than three or four, and when you have a theory you’re pretty sure is correct. There’s actually an entire philosophical discipline dedicated to such scenarios. If it was obvious what to do, the field wouldn’t exist.

“But the numbers are made up”

Perhaps the most serious objection to cross-cause models isn’t “models are dumb.” It’s this: the important inputs are basically guesses. How much does a chicken’s suffering count compared to a person’s? What’s the chance a given AI safety grant reduces catastrophe? Nobody knows. Put guesses in, you get guesses out.

That last part is true. But your gut, even supported by most rational thought processes, still relies on guesses. It just doesn’t label them. When you decide AI safety beats animal welfare, you’ve implicitly answered both questions above. You’ve just done it without noticing, and without checking whether a different, equally reasonable guess would change your mind.

A model can do something your gut can’t: show you which guesses actually matter. Often, you’ll find that the answer barely changes across a wide range of reasonable inputs, so you can stop worrying about those. Sometimes you’ll find everything hinges on one number nobody knows. That’s not the model failing. That’s the model telling you exactly where your uncertainty lives.

A related fear is that the model will say to put everything into whatever has a tiny chance of an astronomical payoff. Naively averaging outcomes can do that. But a model doesn’t have to work that way. You can build in caution about long shots, and many models do. The difference is that a model applies that caution consistently and visibly, rather than whenever the long shot happens to feel uncomfortable. Indeed, the model underlying RP’s Cross-Cause Fund allows just this sort of transparent flexibility to incorporate weight to both long shots and caution about such bets.

Why not use rules of thumb?

Simple rules of thumb can beat complicated models, but mostly when you get quick feedback. A doctor’s checklist for heart attacks is effective because it can quickly determine whether a patient has had one.

Charity decisions don’t work like this. You rarely, if ever, learn if you chose right, the options are hard to compare, and many factors interact.

Yet this is exactly backward to how it feels. The more complicated a decision is, the more tempting it can be to give up on careful reasoning and go with your gut. But complicated decisions are where your gut is least reliable and where it’s hardest to notice you’re wrong. Complexity is the reason to show your work, not an excuse to skip it.

It’s tempting to only follow models when they agree with you

  2. Why it happens: Skipping the spreadsheet feels simpler and more humble, but every gut call is still a model, just one nobody can see or check.
  3. How it goes wrong: The hidden model makes strong claims by accident. An even split says every cause is equally good at the margin. “I’ll adjust a bit for my doubts” could mean very different strategies. Anything you didn’t think about gets counted as zero. A model you only follow when it agrees with you corrects nothing.
  4. Why it gets worse with harder questions: Cross-cause decisions are complex and give no feedback, which is exactly when intuition is least reliable, and mistakes are hardest to notice.
  5. What it costs: Millions can be given with no all-things-considered comparison behind them, so money is likely being misallocated.
  6. What to do: Small donors can rely on a fund or evaluator. Large donors should pay for in-depth analysis, since even a marginally better decision can justify it. Donors in between can use shared analysis rather than building their own. Whatever you rely on, ask it to show its work: which assumptions drive the answer, what’s being counted as zero, and what would change the recommendation.

 

If it’s possible to be famous for your spreadsheets, GiveWell, the charity evaluator, is. To decide whether malaria nets do more good per dollar than deworming pills, they build models with dozens of inputs, such as how many nets are actually used, how common malaria is in each region, and how much a child’s health today affects their earnings decades later.

It’s a heroic effort, built and refined over the last 19 years, that tries to pin down all the uncertainties they have about this complex question.

Now, every so often, someone looks at this complex model and says something like, “Why bother? Malaria kills children. Nets prevent malaria. Worms are bad, but they usually don’t kill you. Nets win. I worked that out in ten seconds from a high-level argument without opening a spreadsheet.”

The problem is that person isn’t truly skipping the spreadsheet. They’ve built one in their head. They just aren’t showing their work, even to themselves.

Congratulations, that was a model

A model is really any story about how an action leads to outcomes. No one opens a spreadsheet to decide when to leave for work. But you have a model: typical traffic, how much lateness you can tolerate, whether it’s raining, and so on. Many people, unfortunately, find out that this is a model when they are an hour late to work because a bridge was closed.

The same issue applies to high-level stories people tell themselves about why to give to one area rather than another or how to split across them. The person assuming “bednets win” has built a model in their head that depends on:

  • Bednets actually being used
  • Malaria being common where the nets go
  • The long-term benefits of deworming being small or unproven, and
  • A child’s life being worth more than a lifetime of somewhat higher income for many children

Each of these is a number. Change a couple, and the answer can flip. GiveWell’s spreadsheet isn’t more complicated structurally than the reasoning underlying the ten-second model. It’s equally complicated, just visible and inspectable.

The lessons here are:

  1. If you disagree with someone’s spreadsheet, you owe them your numbers. “Models are dumb” isn’t a rebuttal when your alternative is a secret model doing computation in your head that can’t be interrogated.
  2. Anything you believe can, in principle, be written down. The real question is whether writing it down loses more than it gains. Usually it gains a lot, and I’m pretty sure cause prioritization is one of those times.

The critics of models have a point, but it doesn’t prove what they think

Some skeptics go further. They don’t just think models are unnecessary; they think models are misleading, and that experienced judgment is the safer guide. They raise some fair points:

  • Point estimates hide uncertainty. Many inputs are best guesses with wide error bars. A spreadsheet that just enters “20%” makes the answer look more certain than it is.

  • The spreadsheet can’t see what it left out. It can carefully track one effect, like lives saved, while missing another entirely, like effects on the local economy.
  • One wrong input can swing everything. A formula error, or even just a poorly calibrated input, can sometimes flip the result.

All of this is true. Now ask yourself whether the alternative of going with your gut fixes any of these issues. Spoiler: it does not.

Even simple cases of weighing multiple views are really complicated. Consider a simple case where you have $10 million to spend on philanthropic causes. You’re about 80% confident in a view on which AI safety is far and away the best use of money. You give about 20% to a more cautious view that proven global health programs are best and speculative AI work might even be worse than doing nothing. In this circumstance, some people think, “I’ll just adjust a little,” and assume they’ve reached the right answer. Unfortunately, that move is almost comically underspecified.

“I’ll adjust a bit for the 20%” could mean any of these:

  1. Ignore the 20%: give the $10M to AI safety
  2. Split by confidence: Give $8M to AI safety and $2M to global health
  3. Follow the main view, skip the riskiest bets: $10M to AI safety but only to established, lower-variance options
  4. Find something both theories can live with: Maybe a mix of $5M to animal welfare (which the risk-taking theory likes) and $5M to global health

These aren’t small variations. These are four different philanthropic strategies. “I’ll adjust a bit” doesn’t tell you which one of these you picked. Worse, there are better and worse reasons to pursue each of these moves in different circumstances; they lead to very different practical results, and it’s hard to do (3) or (4) in a consistent way without a formal model.

(1) just ignores your uncertainties. (2) splits resources. (3) and (4) could result in whatever you want based on how you view the “riskiest” choices and some bespoke informal negotiation in your head.

There’s just no reason to think it’s better to do this type of analysis in your head rather than under a formal structure. And this is the easy case, when you are comparing two theories rather than three or four, and when you have a theory you’re pretty sure is correct. There’s actually an entire philosophical discipline dedicated to such scenarios. If it was obvious what to do, the field wouldn’t exist.

“But the numbers are made up”

Perhaps the most serious objection to cross-cause models isn’t “models are dumb.” It’s this: the important inputs are basically guesses. How much does a chicken’s suffering count compared to a person’s? What’s the chance a given AI safety grant reduces catastrophe? Nobody knows. Put guesses in, you get guesses out.

That last part is true. But your gut, even supported by most rational thought processes, still relies on guesses. It just doesn’t label them. item.title: So you've decided to hire Caroline Ellison. How should you announce it?
item.description:
Published on October 8, 2026 9:56 PM GMT

Two days after announcing that Caroline Ellison had joined Manifund, Austin Chen asked CEA's community health team to 'please let me know if there are things you believe I should do moving forward to mitigate this impact.'

I attempt to answer this question, albeit put slightly differently: if you'd been responsible for implementing this decision, what should you do before it's published?

I'll get my view on the decision itself out of the way first, because it'd be odd to pretend I don't have one. I think it was a bad call. Zachary Robinson's comment makes the principled case better than I could, and Julia Wise puts it more succinctly: 'don't hire someone with a fraud conviction for a finance or philanthropy role.' So I'll add only the practical one, which I don't think has been talked about: it's just not worth the hassle. Caroline Ellison is one person. Austin says he hired her because she was an excellent candidate, and I believe he believes that. But is she so exceptional that nobody else could have done the job? And is she worth all the ensuing very public drama and ostracisation? In my eyes, absolutely not.

But I work in operations, and in ops you regularly get handed decisions you'd never have made yourself. Your job then is to make them succeed, or at least soften their crash landing. So this post is an ops exercise: you're the Head of Ops or Chief of Staff at your org, your founder/CEO has made this call, and you get the Slack message about it. What do you do?

Alex, this exercise is silly, why are you bothering?

This might seem like putting lipstick on a pig. If the decision is wrong, a better rollout doesn't make it right, and I think that's true. Much of the fallout would've likely happened anyway, particularly because some folks believe a hard red line has been crossed (e.g. a recent fraud conviction would disqualify someone from a finance role at CEA).

But the aim of a good rollout isn't to neutralise the harm, it's to minimise it: to mitigate the risks to the organisation, its partners, the people who now have to explain to their own funders why they once used Manifund, and to Caroline herself. And I'd argue that the way the decision was rolled out also did a fair amount of damage, and Austin seems to half-agree. On 5 October he tweeted: 'perhaps I really botched the writeup.'

He also seems, a month on, to be doing several of the things below in reverse order: circulating a private letter to explain himself, running a poll, and considering a large personal donation to settle the $500k FTX lawsuit. Those are all reasonable moves. They'd just have been worth a lot more before the announcement than after it.

Finally, a caveat: this post isn't about how the decision to hire could've been better evidenced or reasoned (e.g. open round, modelling, strict criteria), but rather how the resulting implementation and announcement of that decision left a lot of value on the table.

Anyway, time to be a general after the war. Here's what I would've done.

Step 0: Disagree on the record, then set the conditions for reversal

Before doing anything, tell your CEO plainly and in writing why you think it's the wrong call. This is what disagree-and-commit is for, and it gives the decision-maker one real last chance to reconsider before anything is locked in. If things go tits up, your concerns will be documented.

Then, assuming your CEO is still set on it, I'd do a pre-mortem and agree in advance on the set of conditions that would trigger a reversal of the decision (or at least, further mitigating actions). For example, if specific partner organisations publicly withdraw, or if a set share of balances leaves the platform within three months. Deciding the threshold before the backlash starts matters, because once you're in the middle of the storm you at least have a break-glass plan, which lowers the cognitive load in the moment and makes it easier to overcome sunk costs.

Step 1: Keep the trial internal, then announce on day one

If a hire is controversial enough that you're tempted to give them a pseudonym, that's your signal. You wouldn't give any other new hire one, so the urge is telling you how people will react. The answer is to prepare for that reaction, not to delay it.

The legitimate worry behind a pseudonym is the one Caroline herself gave: she didn't want a public announcement during a work trial, only to be let go a month later. That's fair, and there's a better way to handle it. Scope the trial so that nobody outside the organisation needs to know who's doing it: internal projects only, no customer support, no published writing under the organisation's name. Trialists don't need to face the public anyway, and if you think that's necessary, you've underthought the trial.

Then, if the trial converts, announce on the person's first day as a staff member, alongside everything in Steps 2 to 4, not a month later. You could consider announcing a few days prior to their start date, but it's not immediately obvious to me why that'd be more beneficial (perhaps the pre-mortem exercise in Step 0 or the consultations in Step 3 would make that obvious).

Here's what happens otherwise. Caroline worked at Manifund as 'Carol' from her work trial on 13 July until the announcement on 11 September, including a full month after she went full-time on 10 August. She also published on the EA Forum under that name: Austin noted that 'Carol is the primary author' of a July post arguing that people shouldn't default to starting non-profits, which readers engaged with without knowing who wrote it.

Austin called this a 'minor deception.' I don't think it was minor. Every Manifund user, grantee and Forum reader who dealt with Carol was making a decision without the one fact they'd most want to know. People can only exercise agency when they have full information, and the pseudonym took that away from them. No wonder people are mad.

Step 2: Design the safeguards before you announce

Design the controls first, and publish them with the announcement. Not 'if you're worried, look for yourself', which is what Manifund's announcement offered: 'you (or your LLM) can take a look at Manifund's source code, underlying data, finances and research.' That's a do-your-own-due-diligence answer, and it puts the burden on exactly the people whose trust you're asking for.

It also undersold the problem. The one concrete example of Caroline's work in the announcement is a reconciliation tool that found misregistered transactions 'in the 5-6 figures.' This means she's working on the money ledger (or close to it), at an organisation with two full-time staff, so there's almost nobody to check her work.

Roughly, the controls I'd want in place:

  • Separation of duties. The new hire doesn't approve, initiate or release payments, or change payment details, alone. At a two-person organisation, that means bringing in an outside party, like a board treasurer or an external bookkeeper, to be the second signature.
  • Random review of their work. Periodic audits of code commits and any changes to financial records, by someone outside the organisation. In many health systems, a doctor returning to practice after addiction treatment agrees to random drug testing. It's undignified, but the point is safety, not comfort.
  • Clear limits on the role. Write down what they can't do without sign-off, and publish it.
  • Independent oversight. As user Bland Garlic noted, a competent independent board and someone checking the books are a low bar, and an announcement like this is the moment to show you clear it.

None of this will satisfy everyone. But it shows that the risk has been taken seriously by someone other than the people taking it.

I'd be remiss if I didn't also address the fact that Caroline Ellison is now your employee, and you'll have a certain degree of duty of care towards her as her employer. The above addresses how the organisation will be protected from her, but how do you intend to protect her from the public? Are you including her, to the extent that it'd be appropriate, in the comms planning and strategising? Does she have clear instructions about what her role is during the fallout period, whether she's expected to engage? Have you made adequate provision for mental health support? For all her crimes, Caroline Ellison is still a person, and she deserves to be treated like one.

Step 3: Tell the people who matter first, and give them weeks, not hours

As the ops lead, make a list of the partners, major donors and grantees whose reaction matters most, prioritise the top twenty or so, and speak to each one in confidence a few weeks ahead (ideally together with your founder/CEO). Not a forwarded draft; a conversation. Explain the decision, listen to the objections, take the anger, and change things where they have a point. (Some of their concerns could improve the safeguards in Step 2.)

This isn't about making people feel consulted. It's that people who hear something important at the same moment as the general public reasonably conclude that you didn't think they mattered, and they react accordingly. The ones who've trusted you most deserve to hear it from you first. Some will still walk away, but they'll do it privately and on better terms, rather than in a public comment thread.

This is just good change management: brief the people closest to it before you go wide, so the first time they hear it isn't the same moment everyone else does.

For comparison, as far as I can tell Manifund's advance notice consisted of forwarding the announcement on the Wednesday and Thursday before a Friday publication.   2. Here's what we're doing to address the concerns you've raised.
  3. If there's something specific that would change your view in future, I'd like to know.

While my view of Austin's judgement has severely downgraded, I think it's important to assume positive intent, which I think Austin held at the time and continues to hold. I hope I'm right about that, and I'm happy to be corrected on any of the above.   • Separation of duties. The new hire doesn't approve, initiate or release payments, or change payment details, alone. At a two-person organisation, that means bringing in an outside party, like a board treasurer or an external bookkeeper, to be the second signature.
  • Random review of their work. Periodic audits of code commits and any changes to financial records, by someone outside the organisation.   • Independent oversight. As user Bland Garlic noted, a competent independent board and someone checking the books are a low bar, and an announcement like this is the moment to show you clear it.

item.title: I’m leaving the Center for Reducing Suffering to pursue independent research
item.description:
Published on October 9, 2026 9:44 AM GMT

I have recently decided to leave the Center for Reducing Suffering (CRS) to pursue independent research on the possible implications of UAP and quiet expansionist hypotheses[1] for reducing suffering.

I have some history of writing about these topics (e.g. this essay collection), so this decision amounts to stepping more fully in that direction rather than keeping it perpetually in the background.[2]

I co-founded CRS with Tobias Baumann in 2020, and I greatly appreciate all the support I have received from donors and colleagues while working there. Below, I will briefly explain why I have decided to make this shift.

Why do I prioritize these topics?

Two of the main reasons I prioritize these topics are theory and evidence. When it comes to theory, it seems that people tend to dismiss the possibility of quiet alien expansion based on very strong theoretical assumptions, but I don’t think those assumptions are nearly as solid as people generally assume.[3] In fact, most of the essays I’ve written about this topic (e.g. From AI to distant probes, Silent cosmic rulers, and The cooperative silence hypothesis) argue against the typical theoretical assumptions that supposedly rule out quiet expansion or nearby alien technology. (See also Robin Hanson’s On UFOs-As-Aliens Priors and Aliens Are Not Crazy Unlikely.)

Beyond theory, there is the UAP/UFO evidence, some of which I’ve collected in this post. Despite my strong initial skepticism, I think this evidence is much more notable than one would expect if one hasn’t looked into it. I encourage readers to look into this evidence if they want to better understand this topic, or if they want to better understand my decision.

Another reason for my decision is my sense that I’ve found meaningful insights when I’ve worked on these topics in the past, which suggests that investing further in this area may be fruitful. For example, considerations like those alluded to above arguably reduce the scale of our expected impact and give us reason to focus somewhat more on preventing local s-risks and moral catastrophes, and I think these considerations are worth exploring further. Immense suffering is at stake if we misjudge our situation and misallocate our efforts.[4]

Finally, the area seems highly neglected; it seems like virtually nobody is working on these topics from an altruistic perspective.

Why will I do this work outside CRS?

Given my decision to work on this, I think doing this research outside CRS is a win-win for my research and CRS.

In terms of how it benefits my research, I believe I can work more freely and independently on these topics if I can explore them without worrying about, for example, how my work will reflect on CRS and those who work there. One can see this as a risky research bet, and I think it’s fair that I take this risk chiefly on my own behalf.[5] I would not be comfortable with taking this risk on behalf of CRS, and it would weigh on me if I did.

In terms of how it benefits CRS, I believe my departure reduces the reputational risks associated with UAP-related work, along with the broader set of risks associated with such work. I worry that a strong association with UAP could negatively affect CRS.

I’m pleased to say that my co-founder and I agree that this is the best solution given my decision to work on these topics, and I want to sincerely thank Tobias for his support in my decision. I also want to emphasize that this has been my own decision and there has been no pressure from Tobias for me to leave, only support.

What this means for CRS

CRS will continue to fund research, publish essays, and run courses and internships. Hopefully, CRS will also be able to hire one or more researchers who can contribute to the mission of reducing suffering, with work in AI governance being a strong area of interest. If you think you might be a good fit for such a role, you can register your interest here.

Once again, I want to thank my colleagues and the CRS donors for all their support over the years, and I wish CRS all the best going forward.

  1. ^

    Quiet expansionist hypotheses involve advanced civilizations expanding in ways that are not clearly visible on a cosmic scale.

  2. ^

    This is not a topic I am personally eager to focus on, and I feel real reluctance about doing so given the social and reputational costs. But the potential implications for reducing suffering seem to me too large to ignore.

  3. ^

    Specifically, it seems common to have extreme confidence in loud alien expansion as the dominant mode of alien expansion, despite having little basis for such extreme confidence. See also Freitas (1983) and Kent (2011).

  4. ^

    Just as we can underestimate the scope of our influence, we can also overestimate it, and thereby fail to prevent suffering that we could have prevented with a more accurate assessment of our influence.

    Some have argued for a leverage penalty against hypotheses that imply we have extremely outsized influence over the future, and quiet expansionist hypotheses provide yet another concrete way in which this leverage penalty could be vindicated (in addition to how it might be supported by the simulation hypothesis and by the common-sense idea that large futures will be shaped by many agents).

  5. ^

    Concretely, this means giving up a stable salary and funding the work mostly from my own savings, at least for now.

item.title: How Can We Solve Animal Welfare's Evidence Problem? (Post 1)
item.description:
Published on October 10, 2026 3:10 PM GMT

Many thanks to those who reviewed our drafts. All mistakes are our own.


1. Introduction

Four months ago, Matthes argued that animal welfare has an evidence problem. Discussion mostly focused on the specific examples she gave. Her wider claim received less attention: that the movement lacks enough well-evidenced interventions, and that we need to take ownership of the entire evidence pipeline to change that.

Discussion so far has centred on interventions that are highly invested in, and whether their evidence is strong or weak (the top left of Figure 2). However, Most interventions are neither invested in nor well-evidenced. We want to add a second discussion point: how do we get more interventions to be well-evidenced (ideally, the top right of Figure 2)?

Figure 2: Interventions by movement investment and strength of evidence.

We agree with Matthes that there is an evidence problem. To solve it, we need to rethink how evidence generation works within the animal movement. We need to consider:

  1. What evidence do we need?
  2. What would a movement capable of generating it look like?

This post is part one of a two-part response to Matthes' post. Here, we set out to answer the first question: To define what types of evidence we need and what types of evidence different sources can give us. Part two covers the practical next steps.

2. What Do You Mean We Have An Evidence Problem?

Responding to Matthes, Krzysztof Wojtas argued that evidence-building is not "a linear process", with research finishing before implementation starts. Field implementation is itself part of the learning, and gives different types of evidence that are equally needed.

We agree, and the point exposes a useful distinction: Evidence is not a monolith. Each intervention raises many different questions. Each question calls for its own kind of evidence, and each kind of evidence has its own best source.

Implementation is one of those sources, and it answers some questions well and others poorly. Let's imagine an intervention helping fish in Brazil through improved biosecurity. Here are four questions it might need to answer, and whether its own monitoring data can answer them:

So, monitoring data is an important part of an intervention's evidence sources, but it cannot be expected to fill all evidence gaps. Nor can implementers be expected to resolve all evidence gaps in an intervention. To solve the evidence gap, we will need diverse types of evidence and a diverse set of skills.

The movement's evidence problem, then, is actually composed of many smaller evidence problems, each a kind of question the movement needs to be able to answer about its interventions. To solve it, we need to understand:

  • 1a) What types of evidence an intervention needs
  • 1b) What types of evidence different sources can give us

3. The Evidence Pipeline

So what are the questions the movement typically needs to answer about its interventions? There are many ways to break that down. Here is our first attempt at a framework based on systems from tech development, clinical health, and global development:[1]

Figure 3: The evidence pipeline. Each stage answers a different question about an intervention. As we invest in answering these questions for an intervention (y-axis), the strength of evidence (x-axis) increases.[2] The stages do not run in a strict order: findings at any stage can reshape the others.

item.title: It’s not an ache. It’s a demon from hell.
item.description:
Published on October 12, 2026 7:02 PM GMT

Impressions from the 21st Annual U.S. Cluster Headache Patient Conference, organized by Clusterbusters.

On the morning of the last day of the conference, E. was hanging out with other “clusterheads” outside the conference hotel when he started having a cluster headache attack. Before he could go back to his hotel room, J. offered E. his DMT vape pen. J. is chronic—he gets attacks every day—so he never goes anywhere without his vape pen. He has successfully aborted hundreds of attacks with DMT in the two years he’s been using it. Many years ago, E. had done DMT recreationally, but he had never used it to abort an attack, despite having had cluster headaches for decades.

“Do a 2-second pull, and hold it in as long as you can,” said J. to E. A few seconds later, E. could feel some effects, but the pain was still there. So he took another 2-second pull. He then stared intently at a tree in front of him for about 30 seconds. Then, his face transformed. He smiled, in utter disbelief. He started laughing and crying. The pain was completely gone. He felt clear-headed. He had never felt the pain fizzle away so quickly. The other patients who were there and were familiar with that feeling, offered him a hug. “We know,” they said. “We know.”

"That first time you abort with DMT," J. told me, "it's special. It's very emotional. I think everyone who's done it remembers their first time."

It was not uncommon for attendees to get attacks during the conference in Chicago. There were about 150 patients, many of them chronic or in cycle. As such, there was a room full of oxygen tanks for participants to use freely (high-flow oxygen is the standard, recommended treatment to abort attacks).

Clusterbusters, the leading cluster headache advocacy and research organization, has been organizing this annual patient conference for 21 years. This year, they invited me as a representative of ClusterFree, and especially encouraged me to spread the word about our latest project, ClusterInfo.

It’s common to hear patients describe their first Clusterbusters conference as “life-changing” and even a “life-saver.” Many of them spend years suffering alone, being told by well-meaning friends and family members things like “oh, I also get headaches! Have you tried Excedrin?” It takes many patients a few years to even learn the term “cluster headache.” So, suddenly being in a room full of people who really understand the torture they endure is, to say the least, cathartic.

This was most obvious during the first session of the first day. It’s a tradition to let all first-timers briefly introduce themselves to the rest of the room. The organizers passed around boxes of tissues, knowing there would be tears. And tears were shed indeed—for example, by a man in his forties, desperate to learn more about treatments that could help his teenage daughter, who couldn’t attend herself because she was in poor health.

For me, the conference was special in a different way. I’ve been working on cluster headaches nearly full time for about two years. Before that, I had never met anyone with cluster headaches. In these two years, I’ve met only a handful of patients one-on-one, though I chat with many more online almost daily, for example on the ClusterBuds Discord server (of which I’m also a moderator), on Reddit, and on various Facebook support groups. I think about cluster headaches every day, so being in a room full of the people behind the numbers was a bit surreal.

This was also the first time the conference included a pediatric track, so a few kids attended. While cluster headaches most commonly start in adulthood, a Clusterbusters survey found that about 28% of respondents started getting their headaches before the age of 18. The organizers emphasized the urgent need for more focus on children, sharing the story of an 11-year-old girl with cluster headaches who tried to take her life the day before the conference began.

The second day of the conference featured two plenary sessions on DMT. The first one was a talk by Dr. Erik Zorrilla, who works with Dr. Emmanuelle Schindler at Yale. Dr. Schindler’s team is the only team in the US studying psychedelics for headache conditions. Dr. Zorrilla shared more detailed results from their survey of 88 patients who used DMT to abort their attacks. Some highlights include:

  • 87% reported a complete (100%) or near complete (99%) reduction in pain (70% and 17% of respondents, respectively)
    • 3% reported a 75% reduction in pain, 5% a 50% reduction, 2% a 25% reduction, and only 2% reported it being not effective
  • 76% reported it working in under 1 minute (and 96% in under 5 minutes)
  • 83% reported it working every time without fail (48%) or almost every time (35%)
  • 87% reported it not losing efficacy over time (no tolerance)
  • 53% reported getting other benefits from DMT, such as less anxiety, more energy, or better sleep

If we aggregate the data from all published surveys on abortive treatments for cluster headaches, we get this:

Dr. Zorrilla concluded with two testimonials from the survey:

It’s also worth noting that 85% of respondents reported having some psychedelic effects. In general, a small, sub-hallucinogenic dose is enough to abort attacks, but some particularly stubborn attacks might require multiple pulls, which can induce a hallucinogenic effect. Also, many patients use ready-made vape pens, which contain higher concentrations of DMT because they are made for recreational use. This is to say, we urgently need a non-hallucinogenic analogue of DMT (like BOL-148, a non-hallucinogenic version of LSD that seems to be highly effective at preventing cluster headaches, and whose phase 2 trial has been stuck for years due to lack of funding).

The second session on DMT was a panel discussion with Bob Wold (president of Clusterbusters), Kevin Lenaburg (Chief of Staff of Clusterbusters), and Eric Frey, a patient who had aborted 200 attacks with DMT in his most recent cycle. As he put it, “That would be a lot of suffering without it!.” Bob himself takes a small dose of DMT every night before going to bed, which he believes is the reason he has been cluster-free for the last three years.

Because my team put together a comprehensive guide on how to use DMT to abort attacks, I was given the chance to introduce it. I emphasized the safety chapter, the importance of discussing DMT with their neurologists (if they’re open to it), and the fact that DMT is not a miracle cure (one patient in the audience mentioned that DMT caused his pain to increase). However, the relief is so profound for such a large fraction of patients that not talking about it is not an option either.

Rhonda Pace, a patient married to another patient (they met at a Clusterbusters conference), talked about the role of “care partners,” a term the community prefers over “caregivers,” which implies a one-directional, giver-taker dynamic that doesn’t match the reality of living with someone with cluster headaches. The toll on partners can be enormous, and they also need care. She talked about the daily struggles of living with “the beast.” As she put it, “This is not an ‘ache.’ It’s a demon from hell.” She also emphasized the importance of these patient conferences, which she considers to be a family reunion.

The importance of good support (family, friends, patient groups) became even clearer to me during a conversation I had with Rob, a chronic clusterhead from the Netherlands, over the closing (Halloween-themed) dinner. “Rob,” I said, “I was once asked, if the pain is so bad, how can people endure it day in and day out? You’ve had clusters for over a decade. What would you tell that person?” “Well,” he said, “my wife and kids are absolutely amazing, and while many treatments don’t seem to work for me, my family keeps me going. During a bad attack, I focus on the fact that they, and my friends, and my fellow clusterheads, will be there when the pain ends. And I know the attack will end. It’s the folks who don’t have that support who are the worst off.” Sadly, though, many patients decide not to go on even when those support systems are in place.

Part of me felt very happy that the patients at the conference had this unique opportunity to meet other patients, partners, clinicians, and advocates. Clusterbusters has built something incredibly valuable. Another part of me finds it devastating that millions of other patients around the world don’t get to experience such a bond. My hope with ClusterFree is to reach more patients in countries where care is virtually nonexistent. Bob Wold himself said, “if you think the issues we’ve been talking about in the US are bad—and they are bad—wait to hear what patients who live in Romania have told me. Believe me, you do not want to live with cluster headache in Romania.”

Our project ClusterInfo is one of our attempts to reach such patients. It’s a website with free resources on how to diagnose and treat cluster headaches, currently available in eight languages. Since launching in late May, we’ve already reached over 11,000 unique visitors, and we’re thinking hard about how to make sure that anyone, anywhere searching for information on cluster headaches can quickly find the information they need. We work with patients, clinicians, and other advocates to ensure the content is accurate, comprehensive, and easy to understand. You can find some web analytics here, in case you’re curious.

For our efforts to disseminate information in countries that Clusterbusters hasn’t had the capacity to address, I was honored to receive an award for excellence in education of cluster headache (which would not have been possible without my amazing team and volunteers, and the donors who have bet on us).

There’s so much work to do, though. We’re a team of 1.3 FTE plus a few volunteers, and given how little advocacy and research exists, any marginal effort to support the cause can have an outsized impact. Get in touch if you want to contribute in some way. Or don’t get in touch—just go ahead and do something if you feel called to (including donating to us or to Clusterbusters if you can). I didn’t set out to start a cluster headache nonprofit. For me, it all began when I decided to answer a research question related to cluster headaches, and one thing just led to another. So if you’ve been thinking about taking that first step, however small (and on whatever cause area resonates with you), consider yourself nudged.[1]

Addendum: the Consensus Conference

The two days before the beginning of the patient conference were devoted to the first of three editions of the Clusterbusters “Consensus Conference.” The goal of this conference was to bring selected clinicians, researchers, advocates, philanthropists, and community builders to define concrete, ambitious goals for the next three years.

To put things into perspective, there is currently only one preventive treatment for cluster headache that has gone through the full FDA approval process (galcanezumab / Emgality). And it is only approved for episodic cluster headache patients. There are no approved preventive treatments for chronic cluster headache.

In 2024, the NIH spent about $500k on cluster headache research:

This is not necessarily a failure of the NIH, though. Dr. Michael Oshinsky (Director of the NINDS Office of Preclinical Pain Research, which is part of the NIH) explained that the main reason so few grants have been made to cluster headache research is that almost no one is submitting grant applications. So if you want to get funding for a cluster headache project in the US (or outside it, if you find a US partner), chances are good (and I can point you in the right direction).

While the patient conference was deeply meaningful and rewarding for me, the Consensus Conference, which was more about ideating and strategizing, was very productive. I came away with dozens of new ideas for things to do, from small improvements to our guides to ambitious initiatives that I lack the resources to implement anytime soon. Here are a few:

  • Launch a replication contest with a cash prize for the most accurate visualization of what a cluster headache feels like (see, e.g., this jhana replication contest). There could also be an artistic track, but the main focus should be on depicting the pain as accurately as possible.
  • Host a program analogous to plsdontkillus for cluster headaches. The memetic potential is huge. (Or, generally, try to create viral social media content.)
  • Start more online patient support groups in different countries and languages, like the ones run by Clusterbusters.
  • Do some leafleting about cluster headache. Document the whole process.
  • Try to gather prevalence data from regions with no data (which is most regions).
  • Host patient conferences in other countries.
  • Write a cheat sheet for hospital emergency rooms on how to deal with cluster headache patients, and distribute it in local hospitals.
  • Look into whether impact litigation against insurance companies that deny coverage for, e.g., oxygen could be effective.
  • Create and moderate subreddits for cluster headache in other languages.
  • Create a resource pack, or even just a cheat sheet: “I have a cluster headache diagnosis. What now?” Learn from other conditions (e.g., breast cancer).
  • Create a public ranking of countries, ranked by how well they treat their patients (probably no country would get an “A” or even a “B” as a grade).
  • Try to replicate the HEADACHE Act in other countries.

We plan to gather every year in person and every few months virtually to check in on progress. The excitement and momentum were palpable. I, for one, feel more motivated than ever to get back to work.

  1. ^

     I’ll soon publish a list of ideas for people specifically interested in reducing extreme suffering in humans.

    • 3% reported a 75% reduction in pain, 5% a 50% reduction, 2% a 25% reduction, and only 2% reported it being not effective
  • 76% reported it working in under 1 minute (and 96% in under 5 minutes)
  • 83% reported it working every time without fail (48%) or almost every time (35%)
  • 87% reported it not losing efficacy over time (no tolerance)
  • 53% reported getting other benefits from DMT, such as less anxiety, more energy, or better sleep

It’s also worth noting that 85% of respondents reported having some psychedelic effects. In general, a small, sub-hallucinogenic dose is enough to abort attacks, but some particularly stubborn attacks might require multiple pulls, which can induce a hallucinogenic effect. Also, many patients use ready-made vape pens, which contain higher concentrations of DMT because they are made for recreational use. This is to say, we urgently need a non-hallucinogenic analogue of DMT (like BOL-148, a non-hallucinogenic version of LSD that seems to be highly effective at preventing cluster headaches, and whose phase 2 trial has been stuck for years due to lack of funding).

The second session on DMT was a panel discussion with Bob Wold (president of Clusterbusters), Kevin Lenaburg (Chief of Staff of Clusterbusters), and Eric Frey, a patient who had aborted 200 attacks with DMT in his most recent cycle. As he put it, “That would be a lot of suffering without it!.” Bob himself takes a small dose of DMT every night before going to bed, which he believes is the reason he has been cluster-free for the last three years.

Because my team put together a comprehensive guide on how to use DMT to abort attacks, I was given the chance to introduce it. I emphasized the safety chapter, the importance of discussing DMT with their neurologists (if they’re open to it), and the fact that DMT is not a miracle cure (one patient in the audience mentioned that DMT caused his pain to increase). However, the relief is so profound for such a large fraction of patients that not talking about it is not an option either.

Rhonda Pace, a patient married to another patient (they met at a Clusterbusters conference), talked about the role of “care partners,” a term the community prefers over “caregivers,” which implies a one-directional, giver-taker dynamic that doesn’t match the reality of living with someone with cluster headaches. The toll on partners can be enormous, and they also need care. She talked about the daily struggles of living with “the beast.” As she put it, “This is not an ‘ache.’ It’s a demon from hell.” She also emphasized the importance of these patient conferences, which she considers to be a family reunion.

The importance of good support (family, friends, patient groups) became even clearer to me during a conversation I had with Rob, a chronic clusterhead from the Netherlands, over the closing (Halloween-themed) dinner. “Rob,” I said, “I was once asked, if the pain is so bad, how can people endure it day in and day out? You’ve had clusters for over a decade. What would you tell that person?” “Well,” he said, “my wife and kids are absolutely amazing, and while many treatments don’t seem to work for me, my family keeps me going. During a bad attack, I focus on the fact that they, and my friends, and my fellow clusterheads, will be there when the pain ends. And I know the attack will end. It’s the folks who don’t have that support who are the worst off.” Sadly, though, many patients decide not to go on even when those support systems are in place.

Part of me felt very happy that the patients at the conference had this unique opportunity to meet other patients, partners, clinicians, and advocates. Clusterbusters has built something incredibly valuable. Another part of me finds it devastating that millions of other patients around the world don’t get to experience such a bond. My hope with ClusterFree is to reach more patients in countries where care is virtually nonexistent. Bob Wold himself said, “if you think the issues we’ve been talking about in the US are bad—and they are bad—wait to hear what patients who live in Romania have told me. Believe me, you do not want to live with cluster headache in Romania.”

Our project ClusterInfo is one of our attempts to reach such patients. It’s a website with free resources on how to diagnose and treat cluster headaches, currently available in eight languages. Since launching in late May, we’ve already reached over 11,000 unique visitors, and we’re thinking hard about how to make sure that anyone, anywhere searching for information on cluster headaches can quickly find the information they need. We work with patients, clinicians, and other advocates to ensure the content is accurate, comprehensive, and easy to understand. You can find some web analytics here, in case you’re curious.

For our efforts to disseminate information in countries that Clusterbusters hasn’t had the capacity to address, I was honored to receive an award for excellence in education of cluster headache (which would not have been possible without my amazing team and volunteers, and the donors who have bet on us).

There’s so much work to do, though. We’re a team of 1.3 FTE plus a few volunteers, and given how little advocacy and research exists, any marginal effort to support the cause can have an outsized impact. Get in touch if you want to contribute in some way. Or don’t get in touch—just go ahead and do something if you feel called to (including donating to us or to Clusterbusters if you can). I didn’t set out to start a cluster headache nonprofit. For me, it all began when I decided to answer a research question related to cluster headaches, and one thing just led to another. So if you’ve been thinking about taking that first step, however small (and on whatever cause area resonates with you), consider yourself nudged.[1]

Addendum: the Consensus Conference

The two days before the beginning of the patient conference were devoted to the first of three editions of the Clusterbusters “Consensus Conference.” The goal of this conference was to bring selected clinicians, researchers, advocates, philanthropists, and community builders to define concrete, ambitious goals for the next three years.

To put things into perspective, there is currently only one preventive treatment for cluster headache that has gone through the full FDA approval process (galcanezumab / Emgality). And it is only approved for episodic cluster headache patients. There are no approved preventive treatments for chronic cluster headache.

In 2024, the NIH spent about $500k on cluster headache research:

This is not necessarily a failure of the NIH, though. Dr. Michael Oshinsky (Director of the NINDS Office of Preclinical Pain Research, which is part of the NIH) explained that the main reason so few grants have been made to cluster headache research is that almost no one is submitting grant applications. So if you want to get funding for a cluster headache project in the US (or outside it, if you find a US partner), chances are good (and I can point you in the right direction).

While the patient conference was deeply meaningful and rewarding for me, the Consensus Conference, which was more about ideating and strategizing, was very productive. I came away with dozens of new ideas for things to do, from small improvements to our guides to ambitious initiatives that I lack the resources to implement anytime soon. Here are a few:

  • Launch a replication contest with a cash prize for the most accurate visualization of what a cluster headache feels like (see, e.g., this jhana replication contest). There could also be an artistic track, but the main focus should be on depicting the pain as accurately as possible.
  • Host a program analogous to plsdontkillus for cluster headaches. The memetic potential is huge. (Or, generally, try to create viral social media content.)
  • Start more online patient support groups in different countries and languages, like the ones run by Clusterbusters.
  • Do some leafleting about cluster headache. Document the whole process.
  • Try to gather prevalence data from regions with no data (which is most regions).
  • Host patient conferences in other countries.
  • Write a cheat sheet for hospital emergency rooms on how to deal with cluster headache patients, and distribute it in local hospitals.
  • Look into whether impact litigation against insurance companies that deny coverage for, e.g., oxygen could be effective.
  • Create and moderate subreddits for cluster headache in other languages.
  • Create a resource pack, or even just a cheat sheet: “I have a cluster headache diagnosis. What now?” Learn from other conditions (e.g., breast cancer).
  • Create a public ranking of countries, ranked by how well they treat their patients (probably no country would get an “A” or even a “B” as a grade).
  • Try to replicate the HEADACHE Act in other countries.

We plan to gather every year in person and every few months virtually to check in on progress. The excitement and momentum were palpable. I, for one, feel more motivated than ever to get back to work.
